canonical_question: What should I understand about saturation versus audible distortion, and when is it useful?
clarification_questions: What exactly do you want to change in the a full mix: onset, body, sustain, spectrum, density, peak shape, or perceived position?
Does the problem remain when the processed and unprocessed versions are closely level-matched?
Is the problem present in the source alone, or only in the full mix or after later processors?

competing_hypotheses.description: Saturation versus audible distortion is addressing the intended envelope or nonlinear problem and needs only a bounded amount.
competing_hypotheses.label: Hypothesis 1

competing_hypotheses.description: The audible complaint is mainly caused by level, source, performance, arrangement, timing, masking, or routing rather than saturation versus audible distortion.
competing_hypotheses.label: Hypothesis 2

direct_answer: Saturation is a degree and shape of nonlinear distortion, not a completely separate physical process; the useful distinction is subtle enrichment versus clearly audible waveform reshaping. A practical listening test is: Level-match a barely audible drive setting against a deliberately obvious one, then choose the least amount that creates the intended density in context.

logic_guidance.risk: Louder output can masquerade as warmth, while excess drive can flatten contrast and create grit.

logic_guidance.starting_point: Begin at the lowest drive that creates a repeatable bypass difference, then match output level before judging.

Compensate output level and compare the same musical passage in full context; use mono and quiet monitoring when relevant.

title: Saturation versus audible distortion — what it changes
tradeoffs: Louder output can masquerade as warmth, while excess drive can flatten contrast and create grit.
A louder or peak-reduced version can seem better before the actual timbral or envelope change is judged.
A local improvement can create a new masking, headroom, phase, noise, or arrangement problem.
